content: Syphilis is a complex systemic infection caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum. According to the World Health Organization, at least 12 million individuals globally are currently infected with syphilis. This study aimed to compare the efficacy and safety of two treatments for early syphilis: benzathine benzylpenicillin (commonly referred to as penicillin G) and azithromycin. To evaluate this, a systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Sexually Transmitted Diseases Group Specialized Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, and the Chinese Biological Medicine Literature Database (CBM). The search spanned publications from their inception up to July 2011 and was not restricted by language. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials that compared azithromycin with benzathine penicillin G at any dose for the treatment of early syphilis. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies for inclusion and evaluated the risk of bias. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion. Data from the included studies were pooled using odds ratios (OR) to assess outcomes. Three studies, generating four eligible comparisons, were included in the analysis. One additional study is ongoing. The results showed no statistically significant difference in the odds of cure between azithromycin and benzathine penicillin G. Specifically, the odds ratios for cure at various time points were as follows: Overall odds of cure: OR 1.04 (95% CI 0.69 to 1.56) Cure at three months: OR 0.97 (95% CI 0.62 to 1.50) Cure at six months: OR 1.09 (95% CI 0.76 to 1.54) Cure at nine months: OR 1.45 (95% CI 0.46 to 6.42) Subgroup analyses based on the type of syphilis (primary or latent) and the dose of azithromycin (2 g or 4 g) did not account for the variation in study results. Adverse events were reported in two of the included trials. The analysis of mild to moderate adverse events showed no statistically significant difference between the two treatments (OR 1.43, 95% CI 0.42 to 4.95). However, there was a high level of heterogeneity in this analysis (P = 0.05, I² = 74%). In conclusion, there was no statistically significant difference in the odds of cure between azithromycin and benzathine penicillin G for the treatment of early syphilis. Additionally, no definitive conclusions could be drawn regarding the relative safety of the two treatments. Further research is needed to better understand the utility and safety of benzathine penicillin G for early syphilis.
